title: The top 1% income share is at its highest since 1922
body: India's top 1% income share was 22.6% in 2022-23, the latest year published, up from 18.4% in 2004. The World Inequality Lab puts it at the highest level in its series since 1922, higher than in the inter-war colonial period. The bottom 50% share fell from 18.8% in 2004 to a low of 13.9% in 2017 and was 15.0% in 2022-23.
takeaway: Over two decades the top 1% took a larger share of national income. The bottom half lost ground until 2017 and has recovered part of it since.

title: Formal job coverage fell while the economy grew
body: GDP grew 7.8% in FY26 (MoSPI Provisional Estimates, new 2022-23 base). On the Periodic Labour Force Survey, the share of all workers in regular wage or salaried jobs with any social security was 11.5% in 2017-18 and 9.6% in 2022-23, and GDP grew in every year of that period except the pandemic year. The share recovered to 10.1% in 2023-24, which is still 1.4 points below where the survey began. PLFS starts in 2017-18, so there is no comparable figure for the years before it.
takeaway: Headline GDP growth did not bring a larger share of workers into jobs with social security.

title: Graduate unemployment is four times the overall rate
body: On MoSPI's usual-status series, unemployment among graduates aged 15 and over was 13.0% in 2023-24, against 3.2% for all workers on the same measure. The graduate rate has fallen from 17.2% in 2017-18, and it has stayed three to four times the overall rate throughout. The gap reflects an economy that has expanded low-skill informal work while shedding formal salaried positions.
takeaway: Aggregate labour data masks the structural mismatch facing the educated workforce.

title: India ranks 157th of 180 on press freedom
body: The RSF 2026 World Press Freedom Index, released 30 April, dropped India six places from 151 in 2025. India now sits below Pakistan (153), Bangladesh (152), and Nepal (87). RSF cites concentrated ownership, violence against journalists, and overt political alignment of outlets.
takeaway: India's press environment is now judged worse than that of every immediate neighbour except Afghanistan.

title: India's V-Dem score has fallen furthest in absolute terms
body: V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index: India 0.488 (2014) → 0.260 (2026), a 47% decline and a fall of 0.228 points. Brazil 0.783 → 0.704 (-10%). Turkey 0.252 → 0.110 (-56%). Hungary 0.521 → 0.315 (-40%). South Africa 0.641 → 0.633 (-1%). Turkey falls further in percentage terms, but from a base already near the floor. India's is the largest absolute fall in the cohort.
takeaway: On the most-cited cross-country democracy index, India has erased four decades of liberalisation in one.

title: The Democratic Quality Index is the lowest it has been
body: DQI combines the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index, Freedom House, the RSF rank and the V-Dem Core Civil Society Index through a geometric mean, so weakness in any single dimension pulls the composite down. It has fallen from 0.49 (2014) to 0.29 (2026), against a UPA-decade average of 0.57. The steepest single-year falls come after 2019.
takeaway: No single index tells the whole story, and every credible index points the same direction.

title: Statistical suppression spiked to a peak, then stayed high
body: SSI is a 0-10 weighted sum of graded suppression severities across six documented streams, including suppressed surveys, delayed releases, methodology disputes, and statistical-body resignations. It was 0 across the UPA years. It peaked at 9.0 in 2021-22, when the COVID-mortality undercount (official ~0.5M deaths against 3-5M excess) stacked on the census delay, the withheld consumption survey, the shelved GDP back-series and the permanent merger of the NSSO into the NSO. It remains at 6.4 in 2026, and the 2021 Census is still incomplete.
takeaway: A democratic state is being audited with less independent data than before. The acute events eased. The institutional damage is permanent.

title: Fiscal centralisation is at its highest in the modern era
body: The Fiscal Centralisation Index (FCI) is the mean of six normalised components: cess share, devolution shortfall, conditional transfers, states' own-tax revenue, conditional borrowing, and the structural one, GST, which in 2017 stripped states of independent indirect taxation. On a relative 0-1 scale, FCI rose from 0.19 (2014) to 0.68 (2026), peaking at 0.92 in 2020. UPA-era values averaged ~0.09.
takeaway: GST plus cesses mean states retain less of the divisible pool than at any point since the 14th Finance Commission framework.

title: Central cess and surcharge share of tax revenue tripled
body: Cesses and surcharges are not shared with states under the Finance Commission formula. Their share of gross central tax revenue rose from roughly 8% in 2004 to ~29% by 2024. This is a direct mechanism of fiscal centralisation, separate from changes in nominal devolution rates.
takeaway: A nominally federal tax structure has been redirected by changing the labels on the revenue itself.

title: Reported communal incidents are 40% above their 2004 baseline
body: MHA-reported and independently verified communal incidents rose from 640 (2004) to ~923 (2025). The trend is not monotonic. There is a peak in 2013, a dip in 2016, and steady acceleration since 2017. The series carries a wide confidence band given documented underreporting.
takeaway: Even with conservative counting, the floor of communal violence has risen considerably.

title: Opposition incarceration cases were near zero until 2014, then rose
body: Documented cases of high-profile opposition political figures being formally incarcerated (charged or held in pre-trial detention) were essentially zero from 2004 through 2014. They rose moderately in 2015-2018 and accelerated sharply from 2019, with 9-11 cases per year in 2023-2025.
takeaway: A specific tool of political pressure shifted from rare to routine within a single decade.

title: Exam disruption events have multiplied
body: Documented exam leaks, cancellations, and disruption events across school and competitive exams rose from near-zero in 2004 to ~12 events per year by 2025. The acceleration concentrates after 2018 and reflects both increased reporting and underlying integrity failures.
takeaway: The institutions that gate the labour market are showing visible strain.

title: Open Defecation Free coverage is a textbook logistic curve
body: Verified ODF coverage went from <0.2% (2004) to 98.5% (2024). The growth is the cleanest S-curve in the entire dataset, with a slow climb in 2004-2011, steep adoption in 2011-2018, and saturation thereafter. It is a case study in a state programme that delivered.
takeaway: Where there is sustained political will and clear measurement, India's state can move very fast.

title: Women's labour force participation has risen sharply since 2017-18
body: On MoSPI's usual-status series, the labour force participation rate of women aged 15 and over rose from 23.3% in 2017-18 to 41.7% in 2023-24, and was 40.0% in 2025. PLFS counts a woman who helps without pay in a household enterprise as a worker, so the rate measures participation in work the survey recognises. It does not measure paid employment.
takeaway: The headline rate does not show what kind of work the rise is made of.

title: Gig and platform workers nearly tripled between 2011-12 and 2019-20
body: NITI Aayog estimates 2.5 million gig and platform workers in 2011-12 and 6.8 million in 2019-20, 2.7 times as many. It puts 2020-21 at 7.7 million and projects 23.5 million by 2029-30. This is where employment growth showed up while the formal share was falling.
takeaway: The jobs that replaced shrinking formal employment carry none of formal employment's protections.

title: Rural household income rose 27% in real terms between 2016-17 and 2021-22
body: NABARD's two rural financial inclusion surveys put average monthly household income at Rs 8,059 in 2016-17 and Rs 12,698 in 2021-22, a nominal rise of 57.6%. Rural consumer prices rose 24.2% over the same years, so the real rise is about 27%, close to 5% a year. Borrowing rose too: the share of rural households with outstanding debt went from 47.4% to 52%.
takeaway: Rural incomes grew in real terms between the two surveys, and rural debt grew alongside them.

title: Nine in ten Indian workers have no social-security cover
body: On the Periodic Labour Force Survey, the share of workers who are not in regular wage or salaried jobs with any social security was 88.5% in 2017-18 and 89.9% in 2023-24. It rose to 90.3% in the pandemic year 2020-21 and reached 90.4% in 2022-23. Among regular wage and salaried employees themselves, the share without any social security rose from 49.6% in 2017-18 to 53.4% in 2023-24.
takeaway: Roughly nine in ten Indian workers have no social-security cover, a larger share than in 2017-18.

title: The 2020 GDP contraction was the steepest since independence
body: GDP shrank 7.3% in calendar 2020, the largest annual contraction in India's recorded history. The headline V-shape (8.7% in 2021) masked a structural break. Formal employment never recovered its pre-COVID trajectory, and gig work absorbed much of the displaced workforce.
takeaway: The recovery showed up in GDP and did not show up in employment.

title: India is now the worst-ranked of its peer democracies on press freedom
body: 2026 RSF ranks: India 157, Turkey 159 (essentially tied), Hungary 70, Brazil 80, South Africa 38. India and Turkey have moved together. The others have stayed roughly stable or improved. South Africa is the only peer that improved materially over the period.
takeaway: The relevant comparison set for Indian press freedom is now Turkey. Brazil and South Africa no longer belong in it.

title: Youth unemployment has fallen from 17.8% to 9.9% since 2017-18
body: On MoSPI's usual-status series, unemployment among people aged 15-29 was 17.8% in 2017-18, the first PLFS year, 12.9% in 2020-21 and 9.9% in 2025. It has stayed about three times the all-age rate in every year. The PLFS series begins in 2017-18, so there is no comparable figure for the years before it.
takeaway: The cohort that should be powering growth is the one most excluded from formal work.

title: All three constructed indices point the same direction
body: SSI (statistical suppression) and FCI (fiscal centralisation) have risen sharply since 2014. DQI (democratic quality) has fallen by an equivalent amount. The three are constructed from independent data sources but co-move because they measure related institutional erosion.
takeaway: The three indices are correlated because the underlying processes are correlated. The construction does not force it.

title: The Census is 15 years overdue and counting
body: The last Indian Census was 2011. The 2021 Census has been postponed indefinitely. Every population estimate published since 2021, for ration cards, electoral rolls, sample frames and everything else, is now an interpolation. The compounding error grows every year.
takeaway: India is the world's most populous country and has not formally counted itself in 15 years.

title: The top 1% holds 40% of the country's wealth
body: The top 1% received 22.6% of national income in 2022-23. Its share of national wealth was 40.1%, close to twice as large (Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, World Inequality Lab, 2024). The bottom 50%'s wealth share is below 7%.
takeaway: Within India's already-high inequality, wealth inequality is meaningfully higher than income inequality.

title: A regime comparison, computed live from the data
body: Averaging the data over each regime period: UPA averaged ~7.1% GDP growth, a 20.4% top 1% income share, and a press-freedom rank around 121. NDA's same averages are computed live from the loaded series. Unemployment and formal employment have no series on the PLFS basis for the UPA years, so those two are marked as not available.
takeaway: The regime comparison is mechanical. It averages the data and interprets nothing, and it does not flatter either side.

title: Press freedom and statistical suppression move in lockstep
body: The Pearson correlation between India's annual SSI and inverse press freedom rank is ~0.92 over 2014-2026. Both worsen together. The mechanism is plausible, since pressure on independent statistics and pressure on an independent press serve a similar function.
takeaway: The decline in two ostensibly separate institutions is empirically a single phenomenon.

title: What goes into the Statistical Suppression Index
body: SSI = Σ(severity × salience) / n. Severity scales: withheld (1.0), delayed (0.5), revised (0.3). Salience scales: census (1.0), Consumption Expenditure Survey (0.8), PLFS (0.7), other (0.6). The index is event-based, so a single year's score is the weighted average of that year's statistical incidents.
takeaway: The index is transparent enough that anyone can replicate it from the public record of statistical events.

title: Why the Democratic Quality Index uses a geometric mean
body: DQI = (V-Dem × Freedom House × RSF)^(1/3). A geometric mean is used so that a collapse in any single dimension drags the whole index down, and a country with strong elections but no press freedom is correctly penalised. An arithmetic mean would hide this.
takeaway: Democratic quality is multiplicative. One weak pillar undermines the rest.

title: What goes into the Fiscal Centralisation Index
body: FCI averages five normalised components: share of cesses and surcharges in gross central tax, gap between recommended and actual devolution to states, share of conditional transfers, states' own tax revenue as % of GDP, and overall state dependency on central transfers.
takeaway: The FCI is a snapshot of how much fiscal autonomy states have lost in measurable, audited terms.

title: India and Hungary are now travelling the same road
body: On the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index: Hungary 0.521 (2014) → 0.315 (2026). India 0.488 → 0.260. The two began the period within 0.04 of each other and both ended near 0.3. India's slide started later and travelled slightly further. The Hungary 2010-2024 trajectory has become the most-cited template for understanding India's path.
takeaway: A democracy can fall this far while remaining electorally competitive. Hungary showed it first.

title: South Africa is the only peer that recovered on press freedom
body: 2014→2026 RSF rank: South Africa 42→38 (improved), Brazil 99→80 (improved). Turkey 154→159 (worsened slightly). Hungary 64→70 (worsened slightly). India 140→157 (worsened sharply). The recovery cases share institutional reform processes that the decline cases lack.
takeaway: Decline can be reversed. Peer countries have done it.

title: GDP growth volatility has risen, with larger booms and larger busts
body: Headline GDP growth 2014-2026 has ranged from -7.3% (2020) to +8.7% (2021). The 2017-2019 demonetisation-and-GST window also showed a clear deceleration (8.2→6.1→4.2). The level is high on average, and the year-to-year variance exceeds the pre-2014 period.
takeaway: Average GDP growth is a useful number. For India today, the spread around the average tells you more.

title: Formal job coverage dipped in the pandemic year and has only partly recovered
body: On the Periodic Labour Force Survey, the share of all workers in regular wage or salaried jobs with any social security was 11.5% in 2017-18, 11.4% in 2018-19 and 10.5% in 2019-20. It fell to 9.7% in the pandemic year 2020-21, rose to 10.1% in 2021-22, fell to 9.6% in 2022-23 and was 10.1% in 2023-24. The survey begins in 2017-18, so it cannot show what happened to this share in the demonetisation and GST years before it.
takeaway: The share has not returned to its 2017-18 level in any later year of the survey.

title: Formal job coverage fell by 1.4 points over six years of the labour survey
body: On the Periodic Labour Force Survey, the share of all workers in regular wage or salaried jobs with any social security fell from 11.5% in 2017-18 to 10.1% in 2023-24, a drop of 1.4 points, or about 12%. It did not fall in every year, and its lowest point was 9.6% in 2022-23. Two things moved underneath it. Regular wage and salaried work slipped from 22.8% to 21.7% of all workers, and the share of those employees without any social security rose from 49.6% to 53.4%, after a peak of 54.2% in 2019-20. Over part of the same period, NITI Aayog estimates the gig workforce grew from 2.5 million (2011-12) to 6.8 million (2019-20).
takeaway: More than half of India's regular salaried employees have no social security, a larger share than in 2017-18.

title: India's unemployment rate is close to other lower-middle-income countries'
body: The PLFS monthly bulletins average 5.2% from January to August 2026, on the current weekly status measure. On the ILO's modelled estimates, which put every country on one definition, India's rate was 4.2% in 2025, against 4.5% for lower-middle-income countries and 4.9% for middle-income countries as a whole (World Bank, World Development Indicators, SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS). The headline rate is low because most Indian workers are self-employed or casual and count as employed however little they earn, and because people who have stopped looking for work drop out of the labour force.
takeaway: The headline unemployment rate is a misleading benchmark for India because of the definition of 'employed'.

title: V-Dem score is at 1976-emergency levels
body: India's V-Dem Liberal Democracy score in 2026 (~0.26) is comparable to the score recorded during the 1975-1977 Emergency, when civil liberties were formally suspended. The current score has been reached without a formal Emergency declaration.
takeaway: A democracy can be functionally undone without ever being formally suspended.

title: The bottom 50% income share fell until 2017 and has partly recovered
body: On the World Inequality Lab series the bottom 50% received 18.8% of national income in 2004, 14.7% in 2014 and a low of 13.9% in 2017. The share rose to 15.5% in 2020, which its authors describe as a temporary marginal rise, and was 15.0% in 2022-23. Over the whole period the bottom half lost 3.8 points while the top 1% gained 4.2.
takeaway: The bottom half of India held a smaller share of national income in 2022-23 than in 2004, and a slightly larger one than in 2014.

title: GDP counts the rent on your flat and nothing for the cooking
body: Own the flat you live in and the national accounts estimate a rent for it and add that to GDP. Cook the meal inside it and nothing is added. India's Time Use Survey found women aged 15-59 who do unpaid domestic work spending 289 minutes a day on it in 2024, against 88 minutes for men. That is about 1,758 hours a year for a woman, in no employment figure and no output series. Published valuations of that work run from 7.5% to 36% of GDP. The spread comes from the price put on an hour, and there is little doubt about the hours themselves.
takeaway: The production boundary is a convention. India collects the hours needed to price what falls outside it and does not do so.
